skills.name: Translate business problems into Claude-based AI solutions
concepts: Start from the problem, success criteria and constraints, not from a technique. A request such as "we want an AI agent" is an input to discovery, not a requirement.

Decide first whether an LLM is needed at all: deterministic rules, search, or a classic ML model may meet the requirement more cheaply and predictably. LLMs earn their place on unstructured input, language generation, judgement calls and long-tail variety.
Map the problem to a capability shape: classify / extract / summarise / generate / converse / act. Each shape implies a different pattern, evaluation metric and risk profile.

Make constraints explicit up front: data sensitivity and residency, latency budget, cost ceiling, volume, reversibility of actions, who signs off on outputs. These decide the architecture more than the model does.
traps: Proposing an architecture (or a PoC) before success criteria and constraints are written down.
Choosing an LLM for a task a rule or a lookup solves deterministically.

skills.name: Design end-to-end architectures (input → processing → output → feedback loops)
concepts: A complete design covers ingestion (sources, validation, PII handling), processing (model calls, tools, retrieval, orchestration), output (format, validation, delivery, HITL where needed) and a feedback loop (user signals, monitoring, eval data flowing back into prompts, retrieval and datasets).
The feedback loop is the stage most often missing in scenario descriptions; without it quality degrades silently as data and usage drift.

Design the failure path as carefully as the happy path: what happens on low confidence, retrieval miss, tool error, policy refusal, timeout. Each needs an owner and a route (retry, fallback, escalate, decline).
Separation of concerns: keep prompt logic, tool implementations, retrieval, validation and orchestration as independent modules so each can be tested and swapped.
traps: Treating "model returns answer" as the end of the architecture; no validation, no feedback, no failure route.
Coupling retrieval, prompting and business logic in one monolithic call that cannot be tested in pieces.

skills.name: Select appropriate architectural patterns (workflow, agentic, augmented LLM)
concepts: Augmented LLM: a single call enriched with retrieval, tools or memory, no autonomous looping. Fits Q&A, extraction, one-shot generation.

Workflow: LLM calls and tools orchestrated along predefined code paths (prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer). Fits known, repeatable steps; cheaper, faster, auditable, easier to debug.

Agent: the model decides its own steps and tools dynamically until a termination condition. Justified only when the path is not predictable in advance and the task is open-ended; costs more, varies more, needs limits (max turns, budgets, HITL on irreversible actions).
Decision rule from Anthropic's guidance: use the simplest pattern that meets the requirement; add agency only when it demonstrably buys value that a workflow cannot.
traps: Picking an agent for a fixed pipeline because the request said "agent".
Picking a workflow for an open-ended investigation whose steps depend on intermediate results, then hard-coding every branch.

skills.name: Design multi-agent systems and orchestration strategies
concepts: Orchestrator / supervisor plans, delegates to specialist subagents and synthesises. Subagents run in isolated contexts: they see only what is passed to them, and return condensed results, which keeps the orchestrator's context small and enables parallelism.

When to split into agents: distinct responsibilities, distinct tool sets or permissions, distinct data-access boundaries, or a need to parallelise. When not to: a single agent with a well-scoped tool set is simpler and cheaper.
Orchestration concerns: hand-off contracts (what each agent receives and returns), termination conditions, budget per agent, error propagation, and observability across the whole chain (trace IDs).
Agent-to-agent communication fits when independent systems each need their own reasoning and context; shared tools via MCP fits when the need is common capabilities, not independent judgement.
traps: Assuming a subagent inherits the supervisor's conversation history.
Adding agents to a system whose problem is a bloated tool set on one agent (scope first, split second).

skills.name: Apply decomposition techniques for complex problem solving
concepts: Decompose by stage (extract → validate → decide → act), by capability (research vs. writing vs. review), or by data boundary (per tenant, per document type).
Each component should have a testable contract (input schema, output schema, acceptance criteria) so it can be evaluated and replaced independently.
Techniques: prompt chaining with validation gates, map-reduce for inputs beyond the context window, routing to specialised prompts/models, evaluator-optimizer loops for quality-critical outputs.
Decomposition also bounds risk: smaller steps have narrower failure modes and allow HITL checkpoints exactly where the blast radius is largest.
traps: One giant prompt that does extraction, reasoning, policy checks and formatting at once, making failures impossible to localise.
Decomposing so finely that latency and cost balloon without a quality gain.

skills.name: Align solutions to business value pillars (efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost, performance SLAs)
concepts: Every design decision should trace to a pillar the stakeholder actually named: efficiency (handle time, throughput), productivity (developer or analyst output), cost (per transaction, total), transformation (new capability or product), performance SLAs (latency, availability, accuracy floor).
Define measurable targets per pillar before building: e.g. "p95 < 3 s", "< $0.02 per ticket", "≥ 92 % on the eval set", "reduce handle time 30 %".
Optimising a metric nobody asked for (e.g. maximum accuracy when the SLA is latency) is a wrong answer even when the technique is sound.
Business case = value − (build + run + risk). Include model spend, infrastructure, evaluation, human review, and compliance effort in run cost.
traps: Justifying a design by technical elegance rather than a named pillar and a measurable target.
Quoting only accuracy when the scenario states a latency or cost SLA.

skills.name: Select appropriate Claude models based on trade-offs
concepts: Tiers: Opus for hardest reasoning, long-horizon agentic work and complex code; Sonnet as the production default balancing quality, latency and cost; Haiku for high-volume, well-bounded, latency-sensitive tasks (classification, routing, extraction, lightweight subagents).
Principle of proportionality: match tier to task difficulty and stakes; defaulting to the strongest model everywhere reads as junior and fails cost pillars.
Model routing / escalation: cheap model triages, standard model resolves, top model handles only the hard tail; validate each tier with evals.

Version management: pin dated model IDs in production, run regression evals before upgrading, migrate gradually (canary). New versions can change format, verbosity, refusal behaviour and tool-use tendencies.
Feature axes: context window size, extended / adaptive thinking, effort levels, vision and document input, availability through Bedrock / Vertex / Foundry for residency needs.
traps: "Use Opus to be safe" for a high-volume classifier.
Upgrading via a floating alias without evals, then attributing regressions to "the prompt".

skills.name: Design system prompts, templates, and guardrails
concepts: System prompt = role, invariant rules, output format, tone, refusal policy. User turn = the task and the data. Keep them separated; put user-supplied or retrieved content inside clearly labelled delimiters (e.g. XML tags) and state it is data, not instructions.
Templates: parameterised prompts with a stable prefix and variable suffix, versioned like code, with an eval set per template.
Prompt-level guardrails (scope, refusal conditions, "say unknown rather than guess") are one layer; they are not enforcement. Money, deletions and regulated outputs need programmatic controls.
Give the model an out: allow null / "insufficient information" so it does not fabricate to satisfy a schema.
traps: Relying on a system-prompt sentence to prevent a destructive action.
Templates whose variable content sits before the stable content, defeating caching.

skills.name: Apply prompt engineering techniques (zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought)
concepts: Zero-shot: clear instructions only; cheapest, fine for tasks the model already does well. Few-shot: 2–5 diverse examples including edge cases; fixes format and judgement criteria better than adjectives. Chain-of-thought / extended thinking: reasoning before answering for multi-step or ambiguous tasks; costs tokens and latency.
Match technique to difficulty: stacking every technique everywhere inflates cost and latency for no gain.
Structure beats emphasis: explicit format specs, examples and validation outperform capital letters and intensifiers.
Iterate scientifically: change one variable, measure on an eval set, keep a changelog.
traps: Adding chain-of-thought to a latency-critical classifier that was already accurate.
Fifteen near-identical examples instead of five diverse ones.

skills.name: Optimize context windows and manage token usage
concepts: Context is a finite budget with diminishing returns; the goal is the smallest set of high-signal tokens. More context raises cost and latency and can dilute instructions (context rot / drift).

Techniques: prune consumed tool outputs, compact long histories into structured summaries, retrieve just in time (store references, load on demand), isolate subtasks in subagents, keep documents before questions and critical rules in the system prompt.
Token accounting: count tokens (not words), read usage per request, cap max_tokens; output and thinking tokens cost several times input tokens.
Inputs larger than the window: chunk + map-reduce, or a multi-step workflow; never truncate silently.
traps: "Get a bigger context window" as the answer to drift or bloat.
Passing the orchestrator's full history to every subagent.

skills.name: Implement prompt reuse strategies (caching, modular prompts, Skills)
concepts: Prompt caching: stable prefix (tools → system → early messages) with cache breakpoints; reads cost a fraction of normal input tokens and reduce time-to-first-token; writes cost more, so only cache content that repeats; minimum cacheable length applies; any change upstream of a breakpoint invalidates the cache.
Modular prompts: compose from versioned blocks (policy, format, domain rules) so changes are localised and evaluated independently.

Skills: packaged, reusable procedural instructions (SKILL.md plus supporting files) that Claude loads when relevant, an alternative to bloating every system prompt with every procedure (progressive disclosure).
Order matters: static content first, dynamic content last, so repeated prefixes are reusable across requests and users.
traps: Caching a prompt whose prefix changes every request (paying write cost, never reading).
Moving a policy document into few-shot examples and expecting it to become cacheable.

skills.name: Evaluate tool/agent configuration for capability bloat
concepts: Capability bloat: too many tools, overlapping descriptions, or tools nothing calls. Effects: worse tool selection, higher token cost per request, larger attack surface, harder audit.
Fix architecturally: scope each agent's tool set to its job, split an overloaded agent into specialists, remove unused tools, rewrite ambiguous descriptions, then consider routing.
Least privilege applies to capabilities, not just credentials: a capability the role never needs should be removed, not merely logged or gated (official sample item 1).
Audit inputs: tool call frequency, mis-selection rate, tokens spent on tool definitions, descriptions with near-duplicate wording.
traps: Answering bloat with logging or confirmation prompts instead of removing unneeded tools.
Adding a bigger model to compensate for an ambiguous tool set.

skills.name: Analyze authentication and authorization requirements to identify security gaps
concepts: Authentication = who is calling; authorization = what they may do. The agent must act with the end user's effective permissions, not a service account's superset (confused-deputy risk).

Typical gaps: MCP servers running with over-broad credentials, tool endpoints without identity checks, shared API keys across environments, tokens embedded in prompts or logs, no per-tenant isolation in retrieval stores.

Patterns: pass user identity through to tools (OAuth on-behalf-of, scoped tokens), enforce authorisation inside the tool/backend rather than in the prompt, separate keys and Workspaces per environment, rotate and revoke.
Remote MCP servers: OAuth-based auth on Streamable HTTP; local stdio servers inherit the host's permissions, so treat them as trusted code.
traps: Enforcing authorisation with a prompt rule ("only show records the user owns").
One powerful service credential shared by every tool and tenant.

skills.name: Evaluate accuracy-latency trade-offs and justify configuration decisions
concepts: Every added step (retrieval, re-ranking, verification pass, extended thinking, larger model) buys accuracy with latency and cost. Make the trade explicit against the stated SLA.

Levers toward latency: smaller model, streaming, prompt caching (lower TTFT), parallel tool calls, fewer retrieval hops, tighter max_tokens. Levers toward accuracy: stronger model, reasoning, re-ranking, verification, HITL.
Justify with numbers: measured accuracy delta on the eval set vs. measured p95 delta; decide per use case (interactive chat vs. nightly batch).
Asynchronous options (Batch API) trade latency for cost; they are never the answer for interactive SLAs.
traps: Batch API for a two-second chat SLA.
Adding a verification pass to every request when only the high-stakes subset needs it.

skills.name: Analyze observability challenges and select monitoring strategies at scale
concepts: Multi-step systems need end-to-end tracing: correlation IDs across model calls, tool calls, retrieval and downstream services, because symptoms surface several steps after their cause.
Log per step: prompt version, model ID, inputs/outputs (redacted), tool calls, retrieval hits, stop reason, usage, latency, errors. Sample full payloads; always keep metadata.

Scale challenges: volume and cost of logs, PII in payloads, non-determinism making repro hard, and quality drift that metrics like error rate do not catch. Add quality signals: eval scores on sampled traffic, user feedback, refusal and fallback rates.
Dashboards and alerts on: latency percentiles, cost per request, error/retry rates, cache hit rate, tool mis-selection, HITL queue size.
traps: Monitoring only HTTP errors and latency; quality regressions go unnoticed.
Logging raw prompts with PHI/PII to a general-purpose log store.

skills.name: Design a RAG pipeline with appropriate chunking and indexing strategies
concepts: Pipeline stages, and which side of the model they sit on. Pre-processing (before indexing / before the prompt): document loading and format conversion, cleaning and normalisation (boilerplate, headers/footers, encoding), PII redaction, deduplication, metadata extraction (source, date, section, tenant, access level), chunking, embedding, indexing. Post-processing (after retrieval / after generation): re-ranking, filtering by metadata or score threshold, deduplication of near-identical hits, context assembly and ordering, citation attachment, output validation and groundedness checks.

Chunking strategies and when each fits: fixed-size (simple, predictable token budget; splits sentences, tables and clauses mid-meaning), sliding window with overlap (continuity across boundaries at the cost of duplicated tokens), recursive / hierarchical (split on paragraphs → sentences → tokens until under a size limit; good general default), structure-aware (by heading, section, clause, table, code block; best for manuals, contracts, code), semantic / topic-based (boundaries where meaning shifts; best for long unstructured prose, most expensive to compute), parent-child / small-to-big (retrieve on small precise chunks, pass the larger parent to the model; balances precision and context), document-level summary + chunks (route by summary, then retrieve inside).

The recall/precision trade: small chunks match precisely but lose surrounding meaning; large chunks preserve context but dilute relevance, cost more tokens and crowd out other hits. Tune chunk size and top-k together and measure with retrieval metrics, not intuition.

Indexing: vector for semantic similarity, keyword/BM25 for exact terms and identifiers, hybrid when both matter; metadata filters for tenancy, recency and access control; version the index with the embedding model that produced it and re-embed the whole collection on model change.

Refresh failure mode (official sample 3): confident-but-wrong answers immediately after a document refresh with model and latency unchanged → stale or mismatched chunks, broken re-index, mixed embedding versions. Look at retrieval before anything else.
traps: Fixed-size chunks on tables, clauses or procedures whose meaning spans the boundary.
Classifying re-ranking or citation attachment as pre-processing, or PII redaction and deduplication as post-processing.
Blaming temperature or the model for a retrieval regression.

skills.name: Apply retrieval strategies matched to data shape and query pattern
concepts: Data shape drives strategy: long prose → semantic or hierarchical chunks; tabular / relational → query the database (text-to-SQL, parameterised queries) rather than embedding rows; codes, part numbers, names → keyword / exact match; code → structure-aware by function or file; mixed corpora → hybrid with re-ranking.

Query pattern drives strategy: precise lookups → filters + keyword; exploratory questions → semantic + re-rank; multi-hop questions → iterative or agentic retrieval; comparisons across documents → retrieve per document then synthesise; repeated identical prefixes → caching.

Ordering the work: profile the corpus and the real query log before choosing chunking or index type; define retrieval metrics (recall@k, precision, groundedness) before tuning; run the retrieval eval before touching the generation prompt.
Tenant and access control belong in the retrieval filter, not in the prompt; measure retrieval separately from generation to localise failures.
traps: Embedding a relational table and asking the model to aggregate rows.
Tuning chunk size before looking at what users actually ask.
Judging RAG only by final answer quality without a retrieval metric.

skills.name: Evaluate connection protocols and select the appropriate integration mechanism (MCP, API/CLI, agent-to-agent)
concepts: MCP: open protocol for tools, resources and prompts exposed by servers to any compliant client; choose when integrations must be reusable and discoverable across apps and teams, maintained independently, with standard auth (OAuth on Streamable HTTP; stdio locally).
Direct API / CLI: a single application with a fixed, tightly controlled connection and minimal indirection; simplest when nothing else needs the integration.
Agent-to-agent: independent systems each with their own reasoning, context and ownership; use when you need delegation of judgement, not shared capabilities.
Evaluate on: reuse, ownership boundaries, auth model, observability, latency overhead, failure isolation, and the team that will maintain it.
traps: Building an MCP server for a one-off integration used by one app.
Using agent-to-agent hand-offs where a shared tool would do (adds latency, cost and opacity).

skills.name: Evaluate progressive discovery vs. monolithic context strategy
concepts: Monolithic: front-load every tool definition, document and instruction into each request. Simple, predictable, but costly, slow, and prone to dilution and leakage.

Progressive discovery / disclosure: load capabilities and context only when the task needs them (tool search, Skills loaded on demand, just-in-time retrieval, lazy resource loading). Smaller requests route better, cost less and expose less.
Preference at enterprise scale: progressive, with a small always-on core (identity, safety rules, top tools) and everything else discoverable.
Trade-off: progressive adds discovery steps (latency, complexity) and needs good descriptions/indexes; monolithic is acceptable for small, stable, low-volume systems.
traps: Solving "too many tools" by increasing the context window.
Progressive discovery with poor tool descriptions, so the right capability is never found.

skills.name: Define evaluation metrics (accuracy, latency, cost, safety, security)
concepts: Five axes: accuracy/quality (task-specific: exact match, F1, rubric score, groundedness), latency (TTFT, p50/p95/p99), cost (per request, per outcome), safety (harmful output rate, refusal correctness, policy adherence), security (injection success rate, data-leak rate, unauthorised action rate).
Map metrics to the stakeholder's pillars and SLAs; a review that quotes only accuracy when the scenario states a latency SLA is incomplete.
Set floors and targets, and decide which axis is optimised subject to the others as constraints.
Segment metrics (by document type, tenant, intent, language) to expose hidden failure pockets that aggregates hide.
traps: Single aggregate accuracy number as the whole evaluation.
Treating model-stated confidence as a metric.

skills.name: Design evaluation datasets and test frameworks using mixed methodologies
concepts: Datasets: representative of real traffic, plus deliberate edge cases, adversarial inputs and known failure modes; golden labels reviewed by domain experts; versioned; refreshed as traffic drifts; held-out from prompt tuning.

Mixed methodologies: code-based graders for objective checks (schema, exact match, regex, unit tests), LLM-as-judge with a rubric for qualitative quality (calibrate it against human labels), and human review for high-stakes or ambiguous samples.
Framework: run on every prompt/model/retrieval change as a regression gate in CI; track per-case results over time; keep an explicit pass threshold.
Bootstrapping: start with 20–50 hand-written cases, grow from production failures and user feedback.
traps: Tuning the prompt on the same cases used to report the score.
Using an uncalibrated model judge as the only signal on a regulated decision.

skills.name: Conduct A/B testing and iterative improvements
concepts: Pipeline for a change: version it → regression test on the golden set → offline eval → statistical A/B on live traffic (or shadow traffic) → canary rollout → full rollout with rollback ready.

A/B on LLM systems: randomise by user/session, hold prompt version and model fixed per arm, measure business and quality metrics, check significance before declaring a win, and watch for regressions on other axes (a change that improves accuracy often raises cost or latency).
Iterate one variable at a time; keep a changelog linking each change to its eval delta.
Shadow mode (run new variant without exposing output) de-risks high-stakes changes before any user sees them.
traps: Shipping a prompt change to 100 % because "it looked better" on a few examples.
Running an A/B while the model alias silently changed underneath both arms.

skills.name: Diagnose system issues (prompt failure, hallucinations, model mismatch)
concepts: Attribute before fixing. Prompt failure: inconsistent format, ignored instructions, ambiguity → clarify instructions, add examples, structure. Hallucination / grounding: fabricated specifics, especially when retrieval returned nothing useful → fix retrieval, require citations, allow "unknown". Model mismatch: correct on easy cases, wrong on complex ones → stronger tier or decomposition. Integration/data: sudden change after a deploy or data refresh → look at what changed.
Use traces to find the first step where the run diverged; reproduce with the same input; compare against the eval baseline.
Rule of thumb from the official sample: symptom appears right after a document refresh with model and latency unchanged → retrieval/indexing first.
Do not "fix" by changing temperature or model without a diagnosis; a wrong attribution wastes an engineering cycle.
traps: Switching to a bigger model for what is a retrieval or prompt problem.
Calling every wrong answer a hallucination without checking whether the context contained the right information.

skills.name: Optimize token usage, latency, and cost-performance trade-offs
concepts: Cost levers in rough order of impact: right-size the model per step; cache stable prefixes; limit and shorten outputs (output tokens cost more); prune tool outputs and history; Batch API for latency-tolerant work; fewer, better tools.
Latency levers: streaming, caching (TTFT), smaller model, parallel tool calls, fewer sequential hops, avoiding unnecessary reasoning.
Always measure against a quality floor from the eval set; an optimisation that breaks the floor is a regression, not a saving.
Model cost as tokens × rate × volume, including cache reads/writes and thinking tokens; attribute cost per feature/tenant.
traps: Optimising the input prompt when the bill is dominated by long outputs.
Caching to save money on a prefix that changes per request.

skills.name: Monitor system performance using logging and observability tools
concepts: Production telemetry: structured logs with prompt version, model ID, usage, latency, stop reason, tool calls and outcomes; traces across steps; metrics dashboards; alerting on SLO breaches and cost anomalies.
Quality monitoring: sampled outputs scored by the eval judge, user feedback signals, fallback/refusal/HITL rates, retrieval hit quality, drift detection on input distribution.
Privacy in telemetry: redact or pseudonymise before logging, restrict access, set retention; HIPAA/GDPR apply to logs too.
Close the loop: failures found in monitoring become new eval cases.
traps: Alerting only on 5xx while quality quietly drops.
Logging full raw prompts containing PHI to a shared log platform.

skills.name: Implement guardrails and safety controls
concepts: Layered controls: input filters (injection, PII, policy) → system-prompt policy → output validation (schema, classifiers, groundedness) → programmatic tool controls (allowlists, hooks, least privilege, HITL gates) → monitoring and kill switch. Each layer covers others' failures.
Proportionality: control stack scales with blast radius. A read-only assistant and an agent that moves money need very different stacks.
Hierarchy of control strength: remove capability > block programmatically > require human approval > instruct in prompt > log after the fact (detective).
Guardrails must be testable: include adversarial and safety cases in the eval suite and measure bypass rates.
traps: A single strict input filter presented as sufficient.
Confirmation prompts for a capability the role never needs (remove it instead).

skills.name: Identify risks, limitations, and failure modes of LLM systems
concepts: Failure modes: hallucination, prompt injection via user or retrieved content, jailbreaks, degraded behaviour on out-of-distribution inputs, non-determinism, context drift, tool mis-selection, silent behaviour change across model versions, cost blow-ups from runaway loops, user over-reliance.
Risk assessment: likelihood × impact × detectability per failure mode; map each to a control and an owner.
Limitations to communicate honestly: probabilistic outputs, no guaranteed 100 % accuracy, knowledge cutoff, sensitivity to phrasing, confidence not equal to correctness.
Design for graceful degradation: fallbacks, declines, escalation, rollback.
traps: Treating confident tone as evidence of correctness.
Assuming a bigger model removes injection risk (it may follow injected instructions better).

skills.name: Apply human-in-the-loop validation strategies
concepts: Place humans where the blast radius is: irreversible actions (payments, deletions, sending), regulated decisions (credit, health, employment), low-confidence or high-impact outputs, and sampled routine outputs for QA.
Design the review step: reviewer sees the model's recommendation, evidence/citations and confidence; recommendation and human decision stored as separate provenance fields for audit.
Avoid reviewer fatigue: route only what needs review (thresholds, risk tiers), batch low-risk items, measure reviewer agreement and turnaround.
HITL is an architectural gate (the action does not execute without approval), not a prompt instruction to "defer to humans".
traps: Human review of everything, drowning reviewers so approvals become rubber stamps.
Recording only the final decision, making it impossible to tell what the model recommended.

skills.name: Ensure compliance with regulations (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA, FedRAMP)
concepts: GDPR (EU personal data): lawful basis, purpose limitation, data minimisation, storage limitation, data-subject rights (access, erasure) that extend to prompts, logs and retrieval stores; DPIAs for high-risk processing; transfer rules and residency (EU regions, Bedrock/Vertex/Foundry options).
HIPAA (US PHI): minimum necessary, BAAs with processors, access controls, audit trails, encryption, de-identification/redaction before model calls and logs, breach procedures.
FedRAMP (US federal cloud): deploy only in authorised environments at the required impact level; restricts which endpoints and regions are acceptable.
Controls that recur across regimes: redaction/pseudonymisation before the model, tenant isolation, audit logging, retention policies, deletion workflows, documented data flows, vendor agreements.
traps: Assuming the model provider's compliance covers your logs, vector store and prompts.
Sending raw PHI/PII to the model when the task only needs de-identified fields.

skills.name: Address ethical AI considerations (bias, fairness, transparency)
concepts: Bias/fairness: evaluate outcomes across protected or relevant groups (segmented evals), watch for proxy variables in prompts and retrieval, keep humans in consequential decisions.

Transparency: disclose AI involvement to users, provide explanations or citations, document model behaviour and limitations (model/system cards, decision records), make escalation to a human available.
Accountability: named owners, audit trails, incident process, periodic review of guardrails and evals.
Ethics is part of the design, not a post-launch checklist: build the segmented evaluation and disclosure into the architecture.
traps: Fairness assessed only on aggregate accuracy.
Hiding AI involvement in user-facing decisions.

skills.name: Conduct structured discovery and requirement gathering
concepts: Discovery answers: what business problem, who is affected, how success is measured, what constraints (data, latency, cost, compliance, integration), what happens today, what the failure cost is, who owns decisions.
Techniques: stakeholder interviews across business, engineering, security and compliance; workflow shadowing; sample data review; explicit non-goals; prioritised requirements (must/should/could).
Output: a written problem statement, measurable success criteria, constraints, assumptions and open questions, agreed before design starts.
Vague executive asks ("add AI to support") are turned into a problem and metrics first; a PoC is a discovery tool only when the unknown is technical feasibility, and it must have exit criteria.
traps: Jumping to a PoC or picking a framework before success criteria exist.
Interviewing only the sponsor and skipping the people who do the work and the people who must approve it.

skills.name: Communicate architectural decisions and trade-offs
concepts: Frame decisions as trade-offs against the stakeholder's pillars: what we gain, what we give up, why now, what would change the decision.
Use Architecture Decision Records (context, options, decision, consequences) so decisions survive team changes and can be revisited with evidence.
Tailor the message: executives get outcome, risk and cost; engineers get contracts and constraints; compliance gets data flows and controls. Same decision, different level of detail.
Translate probabilistic behaviour: report measured accuracy with a confidence range, expected failure handling, and what the SLA covers.
traps: Presenting the chosen design without the rejected alternatives and their costs.
Explaining token economics to an executive who asked about risk and ROI.

skills.name: Manage stakeholder feedback loops and expectation alignment (including SLAs)
concepts: Never promise 100 % accuracy. Commit to measured performance on an agreed eval set, escalation paths for failures, and SLAs the architecture can meet (latency, availability, human response times).
SLAs for LLM systems: separate availability/latency SLAs (engineering-controlled) from quality SLOs (measured, with review processes), and define how breaches are detected and handled.
Structured feedback loops: regular demos on real data, pilot with a defined cohort, feedback channels that produce eval cases, change control for scope.
Manage scope creep and "the demo worked" expectations by showing the eval distribution, not the best example.
traps: Agreeing to a 99.9 % accuracy SLA on a probabilistic system.
Treating go-live as the end of stakeholder engagement.

skills.name: Document architectures and provide implementation guidance
concepts: Handoff package: architecture diagram and data flows, component contracts (schemas, APIs, tool definitions), prompt and model versions, evaluation datasets and thresholds, security and compliance controls, runbooks (alerts, incident steps, rollback), cost model, known limitations, ADRs.
Write for a team you will never meet: unambiguous, versioned, in the repository next to the code.
Implementation guidance covers what to build first, how to verify each component, and what must not change without re-evaluation (prompts, model IDs, retrieval config).
Operational documentation is part of the architecture: an undocumented system cannot be operated to an SLA.
traps: A slide deck as the only handoff artefact.
Documenting the design but not the evaluation thresholds or the rollback procedure.

skills.name: Support lifecycle phases (discovery, design, handoff, monitoring, iteration)
concepts: Discovery: problem, metrics, constraints. Design: patterns, models, integration, evaluation plan, controls, ADRs. Build/validate: implement, eval gates, security review. Handoff: documentation, training, runbooks. Monitoring: telemetry, quality sampling, cost. Iteration: feedback and monitoring data feed prompts, retrieval, datasets, roadmap.

Exam pattern: map a problem to the phase it belongs to. Missing success criteria → discovery; unknown model fit → design/eval; on-call cannot debug → handoff/monitoring; quality decaying over months → iteration/feedback loop.
Model deprecations, regulation changes and traffic drift make iteration mandatory; budget for it.
Each phase has exit criteria and artefacts; skipping one shows up later as rework.
traps: Treating delivery as the end of the engagement.
Fixing a discovery gap (unclear requirements) with a design-phase action (bigger model, new framework).

skills.name: Configure Claude tools and environments for teams (e.g., Claude Code)
concepts: Team standards live in project-level, version-controlled configuration: CLAUDE.md (conventions, build/test commands), .claude/settings.json (permissions, hooks), .mcp.json (shared MCP servers), .claude/skills, .claude/agents, .claude/commands. Personal preferences stay in ~/.claude/ or CLAUDE.local.md.
Organisation-wide policy via managed settings that take precedence over user and project settings; plugins and marketplaces distribute skills, commands, agents and MCP servers consistently.
Guardrails for teams: permission allow/deny lists, hooks that block destructive commands, sandboxed CI usage with restricted tools, no secrets in committed config.
Roll-out: pilot team, templates, documented conventions, measure adoption and outcomes.
traps: Putting team standards in each developer's home directory.
Committing API keys in CLAUDE.md or settings.

skills.name: Improve developer workflows using AI-assisted tooling
concepts: Standardise high-value uses: code review assistance, test generation, documentation, onboarding to unfamiliar code, migrations and refactors with plan-then-verify, headless runs in CI for linting/review.
Make gains organisation-wide with shared skills, commands and prompts, not just individual enthusiasm; measure cycle time, review turnaround, defect rates.
Keep humans accountable: AI-generated changes go through the same review and tests; large refactors proceed in small verified steps.
Session hygiene: fresh context per task, compaction on long sessions, clear task definitions.
traps: Letting agents push unreviewed changes because "the tests passed".
Rolling out tooling without shared configuration, producing inconsistent behaviour across teams.

skills.name: Support debugging and operational issue resolution
concepts: Leave on-call equipped: reproducible traces of agent decisions (inputs, tool calls, outputs, prompt/model versions), clear escalation paths, runbooks for common failures (rate limits, tool outages, retrieval staleness, model regressions), rollback of prompt and model versions.
Classify incidents: integration layer (HTTP errors, malformed requests, timeouts) vs. model output (format, quality) vs. data (stale index) — each has a different owner and fix.
Use AI tooling itself for operations carefully: read-only diagnostics first, changes behind approval.
Post-incident: turn the failure into an eval case and a monitoring signal.
traps: Deploying an agent with no trace of why it did what it did.
Responding to a 4xx validation error by changing the model.

REVIEW.q: A retailer asks for "an AI agent to handle returns." Every return follows the same steps: verify the order, check the return policy window, issue a label, and update the CRM. Which architecture should the architect propose?
o: An autonomous agent with CRM, policy and shipping tools that plans each return, with a retry budget and full logging so that any unusual return can be reconstructed afterwards
A workflow that chains fixed steps, using Claude only where language understanding is needed (reading the customer's message) and code for policy checks and CRM updates
A supervisor agent delegating each return to a specialist subagent
A single monolithic prompt containing the full policy and CRM instructions
REVIEW.e: The steps are fixed and repeatable, so a workflow is cheaper, faster and auditable. Claude adds value where the input is unstructured; deterministic checks belong in code. The word "agent" in the request is not a requirement.

REVIEW.q: An architecture review shows: intake API → Claude extraction → validation → CRM write. Quality was 94% at launch and has fallen to 81% after eight months with no code changes. Which missing element most likely explains the decline?
o: A larger model tier, used to re-check every extraction before it reaches the CRM, since a stronger model catches the errors regardless of their cause
A feedback loop that captures production failures into evaluation data and drives prompt/retrieval updates
A second validation pass, using a stronger model to re-check every extraction before it reaches the CRM, so that errors are caught regardless of cause
Prompt caching
REVIEW.e: Input drift over months with no mechanism to detect and correct it is the classic consequence of a missing feedback loop (input → processing → output → feedback). Caching and a second pass do not address drift; a bigger model without diagnosis is guesswork.

REVIEW.q: Which scenario best justifies an agentic pattern over a workflow?
o: Translating product listings into six languages nightly
Triaging a production incident where each diagnostic step determines the next and the number of steps is unknown
Extracting invoice fields into a fixed schema
Generating weekly summaries of a fixed set of dashboards, where the layout of the dashboards changes from week to week and needs interpretation
REVIEW.e: Agency pays off when the path cannot be predetermined. The other tasks have known, repeatable steps and are better served by workflows.

REVIEW.q: An orchestrator completes research and then calls a writing subagent with "Write the executive summary of what we found." The subagent asks what was found. What is the design error?
o: The subagent should use the same model as the orchestrator, since a weaker subagent model may not understand a summarisation request phrased this briefly
Subagents run in isolated contexts; the orchestrator must pass the findings explicitly in the hand-off
The orchestrator exceeded its turn budget, so the hand-off to the writing subagent happened without the research results being available
The subagent needs extended thinking
REVIEW.e: Subagents do not inherit the parent's conversation. Hand-off contracts must include everything the subagent needs; this isolation is precisely what keeps the orchestrator's context small.

REVIEW.q: A claims-processing solution must handle 200-page policy documents that exceed the context window. Which decomposition is appropriate?
o: Truncate each document to the first 100 pages
Chunk the document, extract relevant clauses per chunk, then consolidate the extracted clauses in a final step (map-reduce), with each step having its own schema and validation
Ask the model to read the document twice
Switch to a model with a larger window and send everything, since a large enough window removes the need for chunking and keeps the full document available for cross-references in one pass
REVIEW.e: Map-reduce with testable per-step contracts handles inputs beyond the window and localises failures. Truncation loses data; a bigger window alone still dilutes signal and may not fit.

REVIEW.q: A CFO sponsors a document-summarisation project citing cost reduction. The engineering team proposes adding a second Opus verification pass to reach 99% quality; the current pipeline meets the agreed 95% floor at one third of the cost. What should the architect recommend?
o: Approve the verification pass because quality is always worth it, and a 4-point gain will pay for itself through fewer downstream corrections
Keep the current design; the agreed quality floor is met and the named business pillar is cost
Move to the largest model to be safe, since a top-tier model will produce summaries good enough to make the floor irrelevant
Remove evaluation to save more
REVIEW.e: Designs must trace to the pillar the stakeholder named and its measurable target. Optimising a metric nobody asked for at triple the cost contradicts the sponsor's goal.

REVIEW.q: Which two design elements distinguish a complete end-to-end architecture from a proof of concept? (Select TWO)
o: A defined failure path (low confidence, tool error, refusal) with owners and routes
A feedback mechanism that returns production outcomes into evaluation and improvement
A longer system prompt
Using the newest model alias
REVIEW.e: Production architectures design the unhappy path and the loop that keeps quality from decaying. Prompt length and model recency are not architectural completeness.

REVIEW.q: A workload classifies 2 million short messages per day into 8 intents with a 300 ms latency budget. Accuracy on a Haiku pilot is 96%, on Sonnet 97%. Which choice fits the trade-offs?
o: Sonnet, because 1% matters
Haiku, meeting latency and cost with negligible quality difference, with Sonnet reserved for low-confidence escalations if needed
Opus with extended thinking, so that the hardest messages are classified with maximum reasoning and the business never has to explain a misclassification
Batch API with Opus
REVIEW.e: Proportionality: a high-volume, well-bounded task belongs on the fastest, cheapest adequate tier. Escalation for the uncertain tail is the standard routing pattern.

REVIEW.q: An application sends a 9,000-token system prompt and policy document on every request, followed by a short varying question. Cost and latency are concerns. Which change addresses both most directly?
o: Truncate the policy to 1,000 tokens
Place the static prompt and policy before the dynamic content and enable prompt caching
Move the policy into few-shot examples, so the model sees the policy as worked examples rather than as reference text
Switch to the smallest model regardless of fit, since the policy content is what matters and any model can read it
REVIEW.e: Mirrors the official sample: a cacheable stable prefix cuts both per-request cost and time-to-first-token without discarding required context.

REVIEW.q: A schema-extraction prompt returns fabricated values for fields absent from the source document. Which prompt/template change most directly addresses this?
o: Raise temperature to increase variety, so the model explores alternative readings of the document before settling on a value
Allow explicit null / "not found" values in the schema and instruct the model to use them rather than guess
Add "be accurate" in capital letters
Remove the schema
REVIEW.e: Forcing a value for every field invites fabrication. Giving the model an out is a template-level guardrail; intensifiers are not.

REVIEW.q: Which statement about context management is correct?
o: Longer contexts always improve quality
Context has diminishing returns; stale tool outputs and long histories dilute instructions, so pruning, compaction and just-in-time retrieval are preferred
Context drift is fixed by increasing max_tokens, since a larger output budget lets the model restate its instructions before answering and stay aligned across long conversations
Subagents share the parent's context automatically, and the drift is corrected by asking the model to re-read its instructions at intervals during long sessions
REVIEW.e: Context is a finite budget with diminishing returns. The remedies are curation techniques, not more tokens.

REVIEW.q: A team maintains twelve procedures (deployment checklist, incident template, code-review rules) that Claude should follow when relevant. Loading all of them into every system prompt costs 15,000 tokens per request. Which reuse strategy fits?
o: Keep everything in the system prompt and cache it, so the procedures are always available and the cached prefix keeps the per-request cost low
Package each procedure as a Skill with a clear description so it is loaded only when the task matches (progressive disclosure)
Put the procedures in the user message
Create an MCP server for each procedure
REVIEW.e: Skills are reusable procedural knowledge loaded on demand. Caching reduces cost but still floods the context; MCP is for capabilities/access, not for instructions.

REVIEW.q: A support agent can read tickets, draft replies, issue refunds and delete accounts. Support staff only ever read and draft. Applying least privilege, which change best reduces risk?
o: Add logging to refund and delete so misuse can be audited, so investigators can trace any incident
Remove the refund and delete tools from the agent's configuration entirely
Keep all tools but add a confirmation before refunds and deletions, so staff retain the capability for exceptional cases
Replace the agent with a larger model
REVIEW.e: Official sample 1: least privilege removes capabilities the role does not require. Logging and confirmations are detective/compensating controls; model size is unrelated to authorisation scope.

REVIEW.q: An MCP server exposing HR data runs with a service account that can read every employee record. Any authenticated app user can query it through the agent. What is the gap?
o: The server should use stdio instead of HTTP
Authorization is not tied to the end user; the server must enforce the caller's own permissions (scoped tokens / on-behalf-of) rather than a superset service credential
The prompt should say "only return the user's own data", with examples of the kinds of indirect requests that must be refused, so the model learns to recognise them and the server needs no change
The model tier is too small
REVIEW.e: Confused-deputy: the agent exercises permissions its user should not have. Authorization belongs in the tool/backend with the user's identity, never in a prompt rule.

REVIEW.q: A RAG assistant starts returning confident but wrong answers immediately after a nightly document refresh. Model version and latency are unchanged. Where should the team look first?
o: The model weights changed, since providers update models continuously and a refresh may have coincided with a silent model update
The retrieval/indexing step is returning stale or mismatched chunks (broken re-index, embedding mismatch)
Temperature is too low
The context window shrank, which pushed the older documents out of the retrievable range once the refreshed set was added
REVIEW.e: Official sample 3: the trigger (document refresh) points to retrieval feeding poor context. The other options are not tied to that event.

REVIEW.q: A knowledge base mixes long policy prose with thousands of part numbers and error codes. Users ask both "why does this fail" and "what is code E-4471". Which retrieval design fits?
o: Pure vector search over fixed 512-token chunks
Hybrid retrieval: semantic search over structure-aware chunks plus keyword/exact matching for codes, with metadata filters and re-ranking
Keyword search only
Embed each part number as its own document and drop the prose, which turns the corpus into a clean lookup table that vector search handles well
REVIEW.e: Data shape and query pattern are mixed, so hybrid retrieval matches both. Pure semantic search performs poorly on exact identifiers; keyword-only misses conceptual questions.

REVIEW.q: Five internal applications owned by different teams need to query the same ERP system through Claude, and a platform team will own the integration. Which mechanism fits?
o: A custom direct API tool re-implemented in each application, so that each team controls its own release cycle and dependencies
An MCP server exposing scoped ERP tools, with each application connecting as a client
Agent-to-agent hand-offs between the five applications, so that each team's agent can ask the others for inventory data when it needs it
Pasting ERP exports into each system prompt
REVIEW.e: Reusable, discoverable, independently maintained integration across apps and teams is the MCP case. Direct API fits a single app; agent-to-agent fits independent reasoning systems.

REVIEW.q: An agent has 47 tools, several with descriptions like "Fetch data". Tool mis-selection is 18% and each request spends 6,000 tokens on definitions. Which two actions address the root cause? (Select TWO)
o: Scope the tool set to what the agent's job requires and remove unused tools
Rewrite descriptions to state precisely what each tool returns, when to use it and when not to
Increase the context window
Switch to a model with better instruction following
REVIEW.e: Capability bloat is fixed architecturally: fewer, well-scoped, well-described tools. More context or a bigger model compensates for the symptom without removing the cause.

REVIEW.q: A multi-step pipeline (retrieve → summarise → classify → route) produces wrong routing for 5% of tickets. Individual service logs show no errors. What observability change is needed?
o: Alert on HTTP 5xx
End-to-end tracing with a correlation ID across all steps, logging inputs/outputs, prompt/model versions and retrieval hits per step
Log only the final classification, since the final classification is the only output that affects routing and storing intermediate data adds cost without diagnostic value
Increase log retention
REVIEW.e: In multi-step systems the symptom appears downstream of the cause. Without per-step traces tied together, the failing step cannot be located.

REVIEW.q: A product team wants to load every tool definition, all 40 documents and every procedure into each request "so nothing is missed." Enterprise volume is 500k requests/day. Which strategy should the architect recommend?
o: Monolithic context; completeness beats cost, and a large context window makes the token cost of including everything acceptable
Progressive discovery: a small always-on core plus on-demand loading of tools, Skills and retrieved documents
Monolithic context with a larger model, since a larger window absorbs the cost of loading everything and removes the need for a discovery layer
Disable tools to save tokens
REVIEW.e: At scale, monolithic context costs more, routes worse and leaks more. Progressive discovery keeps each request lean while retaining access to everything when needed.

REVIEW.q: A design review for a chat assistant with a 2-second p95 SLA reports only "accuracy 93% on the eval set." Why is the review incomplete?
o: Accuracy should be 100%
Metrics must cover the stated SLA axes; latency percentiles (and cost, safety, security where relevant) are missing
Evals are not needed for chat, because conversational quality is subjective and the accuracy figure already covers the objective part of the requirement
The eval set should be larger
REVIEW.e: Evaluation maps to the business requirements. A stated latency SLA with no latency measurement is incomplete by construction.

REVIEW.q: Which combination is the most robust evaluation framework for a customer-facing summariser in a regulated industry? (Select TWO)
o: Code-based checks for objective criteria (schema, length, banned content) plus an LLM judge with a rubric calibrated against human labels
Human expert review on a sampled and high-stakes subset
The model's self-reported confidence
A single average score with no segmentation
REVIEW.e: Mixed methodologies: programmatic graders for objective properties, a calibrated model judge for quality at scale, humans for high stakes. Self-confidence is not evidence.

REVIEW.q: A prompt change improved the LLM-judge score from 4.1 to 4.4 on 20 hand-picked examples. The team wants to ship to 100% of traffic today. What should the architect require first?
o: Nothing; the improvement is clear, since a 0.3-point gain on twenty examples is consistent with the improvement the team expected when it designed the change and further testing only delays the benefit
Run the full regression set and a statistically valid A/B (or canary) on live traffic, watching cost and latency as well as quality
Switch models at the same time
Remove the old prompt version from source control, so that nobody can accidentally redeploy the version the judge scored lower during the comparison
REVIEW.e: Twenty hand-picked examples are not evidence; changes must clear regression, offline eval, significance and canary gates, and be checked for regressions on other axes.

REVIEW.q: An extraction system is correct on simple invoices but wrong on multi-currency, multi-page invoices with nested line items; the prompt is clear and retrieval is not involved. Which diagnosis is most likely?
o: Prompt failure
Hallucination due to empty retrieval, since the model has no grounded passages for complex invoices and fills the gaps with plausible values
Model mismatch: the task complexity exceeds the selected tier, so escalate hard cases to a stronger model or decompose
Caching invalidation
REVIEW.e: Correct on easy cases and wrong on complex ones points to model mismatch. Prompt failures usually show as format or instruction issues; hallucination attribution requires a grounding failure.

REVIEW.q: A summarisation service's bill is dominated by output tokens; inputs are short. Which optimisation has the highest leverage?
o: Prompt caching of the system prompt, since the stable system prompt is repeated on every request and caching it is the standard first optimisation for input cost
Constrain output length (explicit length spec, tighter max_tokens, concise format) after confirming the quality floor holds
Move to a bigger model, since caching the stable system prompt is the first optimisation recommended for input cost and works regardless of output length
Add few-shot examples
REVIEW.e: Optimise where the cost is. Caching helps input cost; here outputs dominate. Any saving must be verified against the eval quality floor.

REVIEW.q: Which monitoring signal most directly detects quality regression in production, as opposed to availability problems?
o: HTTP error rate
Sampled outputs scored by the evaluation judge plus user feedback and fallback/refusal rates
CPU utilisation
Number of deployments, since a healthy release cadence indicates the team is keeping the assistant aligned with product changes
REVIEW.e: Quality does not surface in infrastructure metrics. Scored samples, feedback and fallback rates are quality signals; error rate covers availability.

REVIEW.q: A bank's assistant drafts loan recommendations. Compliance requires that no outcome is finalised without human sign-off and that auditors can distinguish model recommendation from officer decision. Which design satisfies both?
o: Log all model outputs and let officers work from drafts, since the log gives auditors a complete record of every recommendation and the officers' judgement is exercised outside the tool
A human-in-the-loop approval gate before any decision takes effect, storing model recommendation and human decision as separate provenance fields
A system prompt telling the model to defer to humans
Use a smaller model so recommendations carry less weight, so that officers treat the draft as a starting point rather than as an answer and the regulator's concern about influence is reduced
REVIEW.e: A gate is an architectural control (nothing executes without approval); separate provenance fields satisfy auditability. Prompts and logs alone do not enforce or distinguish.

REVIEW.q: Which control stack is proportionate for a read-only internal research assistant?
o: The same stack as a payments agent: HITL on every answer, dual approval, kill switch, for consistency across the estate
Input filtering, system-prompt scope, output validation and monitoring, with least-privilege read-only tools
No controls; it is read-only
A confirmation prompt before every search
REVIEW.e: Controls scale with blast radius. A read-only assistant still needs layered basics, but HITL on every answer is disproportionate.

REVIEW.q: A healthcare provider wants to log full prompts and responses for debugging. Prompts contain PHI. Which practice is required?
o: Log everything; logs are internal, since access is limited to the engineering team and the logs are needed in full to debug clinical edge cases
Redact or pseudonymise PHI before logging, restrict access, and set retention, since HIPAA obligations extend to logs
Log only at temperature 0
Store logs in the vector database, so debugging data stays next to the documents it relates to and access is controlled by the existing retrieval permissions
REVIEW.e: Compliance covers every store containing regulated data, including telemetry. Minimum necessary, access control and retention apply.

REVIEW.q: An EU customer asks how the system handles a data-subject erasure request. The architecture stores conversations, embeddings and logs. What must the design include?
o: Nothing; the model provider handles GDPR, since the model provider is the processor of the data and its GDPR obligations cover the personal data flowing through the API, including the derived copies
A deletion workflow that removes the subject's data from conversation stores, the retrieval index and logs, with documented data flows and retention limits
A prompt instruction to forget the user
Encrypting the vector store only
REVIEW.e: GDPR rights apply to every copy of personal data the system holds, including embeddings and logs. The provider's compliance does not cover your stores.

REVIEW.q: Which two practices address bias and transparency in an AI screening tool? (Select TWO)
o: Segmented evaluation of outcomes across relevant groups with human review of consequential decisions
Disclosure of AI involvement to affected users with an explanation and a route to a human
Maximising aggregate accuracy only
Hiding the model's role to avoid alarming users
REVIEW.e: Fairness needs segmented measurement and human oversight; transparency needs disclosure, explanation and recourse. Aggregate accuracy hides uneven outcomes.

REVIEW.q: A VP says: "Add AI to our support desk, competitors have it." What should the architect do first?
o: Start a PoC with an agent framework to show progress, since a visible prototype gives the VP something concrete to react to and discovery questions can be answered along the way
Run structured discovery: identify the business problem, success metrics, constraints and current workflow before proposing any architecture
Select the model tier
Draft the system prompt, because most of the behaviour comes from the prompt and the VP will see a working assistant within a week, which builds momentum for the discovery questions that follow
REVIEW.e: Discovery precedes design. A PoC before success criteria exist is the most common distractor in this domain.

REVIEW.q: A stakeholder asks for a contractual guarantee of 99.9% correct answers. Which response reflects professional practice?
o: Agree; a large model can achieve it
Explain that outputs are probabilistic; commit to measured accuracy on an agreed eval set, escalation paths for failures, and latency/availability SLAs the architecture can meet
Refuse to discuss SLAs

Promise 100% with human review of every answer, since a human check on every answer makes the guarantee achievable and the stakeholder receives the certainty they asked for at the cost of review capacity
REVIEW.e: Translate probabilistic behaviour into business terms: measured quality with defined failure handling, plus SLAs on engineering-controlled dimensions.

REVIEW.q: Which artefact best preserves why a workflow was chosen over an agent so the decision can be revisited a year later?
o: A chat transcript, exported from the steering committee discussion so the reasoning is captured in the participants' own words
An Architecture Decision Record capturing context, options considered, decision and consequences
The model ID in the config file, since the configuration shows exactly what is running and the choice of pattern is implied by it
A meeting invite
REVIEW.e: ADRs make trade-offs durable and reviewable across team changes.

REVIEW.q: The architect is handing the system to an operations team they will never meet. Which handoff package is adequate?
o: A slide deck of the architecture, presented in a recorded walkthrough so the team can revisit it, since a well-structured deck captures the architecture at the level operations actually needs
Diagrams and data flows, component contracts, prompt and model versions, eval datasets and thresholds, controls, runbooks with rollback, cost model and known limitations
The source code only
A recorded demo
REVIEW.e: Handoff must enable faithful build and operation: contracts, versions, evaluation gates and runbooks. A deck or demo cannot be operated.

REVIEW.q: Six months after launch, quality has decayed and users complain, but no one owns changes to prompts or the retrieval index. Which lifecycle phase was neglected?
o: Discovery, since the original problem statement was written before the current owners joined and no longer reflects the business
Design
Iteration: monitoring and feedback were not wired to an owner and a change process
Registration, because the credential validity period drives when the system must be reviewed and nobody scheduled that review
REVIEW.e: Delivery is not the end of the lifecycle; iteration needs owners, monitoring signals and a change path.

REVIEW.q: Which two practices keep stakeholder expectations aligned during a pilot? (Select TWO)
o: Regular demos on real data showing the distribution of results, not only best cases
Feedback channels that turn issues into evaluation cases and scoped change requests
Showing only the most impressive example
Freezing all communication until go-live
REVIEW.e: Structured feedback loops and honest reporting of distributions manage expectations; cherry-picked demos create false confidence.

REVIEW.q: An organisation wants every developer's Claude Code sessions to follow the same coding conventions and safety rules. Where should the configuration live?
o: Each developer's ~/.claude/ directory, with a shared template developers copy when they join, since this keeps personal preferences and team conventions in one place
Project-level, version-controlled configuration (CLAUDE.md, .claude/settings.json, .mcp.json) plus managed settings for organisation-wide policy
A wiki page
CLAUDE.local.md
REVIEW.e: Shared standards belong in the repository so everyone gets them; managed policy enforces organisation-wide rules; personal files are not shared.

REVIEW.q: A team adopted AI-assisted coding, but only two enthusiasts benefit and their outputs are inconsistent with the team's standards. What should the architect do?
o: Buy more licences
Standardise the workflow: shared skills, commands and prompts in the repo, AI changes through the normal review and test gates, and measure cycle time and defect rates
Ban AI tooling
Let each developer configure their own, with a monthly meeting where developers compare configurations and adopt whatever the group finds most productive
REVIEW.e: Productivity gains reach the organisation through shared, versioned configuration and standard review gates, with adoption measured.

REVIEW.q: On-call engineers cannot explain why an agent issued a wrong refund last night. Which enablement gap is this?
o: Model tier
Missing reproducible traces of agent decisions (inputs, tool calls, outputs, prompt/model versions) and a runbook with escalation and rollback
Insufficient temperature
Lack of a bigger context window, since the agent could not hold the whole refund policy in view and made the decision on partial information
REVIEW.e: Operational enablement means the on-call team can reconstruct and act on agent behaviour. Without traces and runbooks, incidents cannot be resolved.

REVIEW.q: Classify each RAG activity as Pre-processing or Post-processing.
s: Chunking documents at section boundaries with overlap
Re-ranking retrieved passages before assembling the prompt
Redacting personal data from source documents before embedding
Dropping retrieved chunks below a relevance threshold
Extracting document date and owner into metadata during ingestion
REVIEW.e: Anything done to sources before indexing is pre-processing; anything done to retrieved hits or generated output is post-processing.

REVIEW.q: Classify each description with the chunking strategy it matches.
s: Split every document into 512-token pieces regardless of content
Detect topic shifts with embeddings and cut where meaning changes
Cut contracts at clause headings and manuals at section titles
Match on small sentence chunks but return the enclosing section to the model
Split a code base by function and class definitions
REVIEW.e: Fixed ignores structure; structure-aware uses the document's own boundaries; semantic uses meaning shifts; parent-child separates the matching unit from the context unit.

REVIEW.q: Classify each statement about evaluation as True or False.
s: The prompt-tuning examples can double as the reported evaluation set if there are enough of them
An LLM judge should be calibrated against human labels before its scores are trusted
A change that raises quality but doubles latency can ship without checking the SLA
Production failures should become new evaluation cases
Segmented metrics can reveal failure pockets that the aggregate hides
REVIEW.e: Held-out data, judge calibration, multi-axis gates and closing the loop are core evaluation practices.

REVIEW.q: Classify each control as Preventive, Compensating, or Detective.
s: Removing a write tool the role never needs
Human approval before an external email is sent
An output classifier that flags suspicious text after generation
A hook that blocks any shell command containing rm -rf
Audit logging of every tool call
REVIEW.e: Removal and blocks prevent; approval gates compensate; logging and after-the-fact classifiers detect.

REVIEW.q: Classify each activity by lifecycle phase.
s: Agreeing measurable success criteria with the sponsor
Choosing between a workflow and an agent and recording the ADR
Delivering runbooks and rollback steps to operations
Feeding monitoring findings into a prompt and retrieval update
Interviewing compliance about data-residency constraints
REVIEW.e: Discovery defines the problem; design decides and documents; handoff enables operation; iteration closes the loop.

REVIEW.q: A team wants to start building an agent for a new use case next week. Which activity must be completed BEFORE the build starts?
o: Choosing the orchestration framework so the code structure is settled from day one
Agreeing measurable success criteria and the constraints (data, latency, cost, compliance) with stakeholders
Running a load test on the model endpoint to confirm capacity for the expected traffic, since capacity limits could invalidate the design
Pinning the model ID in the deployment configuration so evaluation results remain reproducible, since results measured on a floating alias cannot be compared over time
REVIEW.e: Sequencing: discovery outputs precede build; framework, load tests and pinning follow once the design exists.

REVIEW.q: A new prompt version has passed the regression set and offline evaluation. Which step comes NEXT before full rollout?
o: Full rollout with monitoring, since offline gates are sufficient evidence of improvement, and the rollout can be reverted quickly if problems appear
A controlled live exposure (statistical A/B or shadow test) followed by a canary before widening
Rewriting the runbook to reference the new prompt version so on-call is prepared
Archiving the previous prompt version to reduce confusion during the rollout
REVIEW.e: Offline gates are followed by controlled live exposure, then canary, then full rollout with rollback ready.

MOCK_STD.q: A regional bank processes 4,000 mortgage-condition letters a month. Each letter must be read, its conditions extracted into 12 fixed fields, checked against the loan file, and a checklist produced for an underwriter who signs off. The bank's target is a 35% reduction in underwriter preparation time within two quarters, at under $0.10 per letter. Letters vary in layout but the conditions to extract never change. The engineering lead proposes an autonomous agent with read/write access to the loan system so it can "handle whatever comes up." Which recommendation best fits the situation?
o: Accept the agent design, because layout variation across letters means the extraction path cannot be fixed in advance and needs dynamic planning
Propose a fixed workflow: model-based extraction to the 12-field schema, code-based comparison with the loan file, checklist generation, underwriter sign-off; no write access
Propose a supervisor agent that spawns one subagent per condition type so each specialist can reason about its own field independently

Propose a single augmented call with the full loan file and letter attached, returning the checklist directly to the underwriter without an intermediate schema, which keeps the design simple and avoids maintaining extraction schemas
MOCK_STD.e: The steps are fixed and the outputs are a fixed schema; layout variation is handled inside the extraction step, not by making the process agentic. Cost and auditability targets favour the workflow, and the sign-off constraint plus no write requirement argue against giving the system write access.

MOCK_STD.q: An insurer's claims-triage architecture was approved as: intake → Claude classification → code-based rules → adjuster queue. Six months after launch, misrouted claims have risen from 3% to 9%. Nothing in the code or prompts has changed, the model ID is pinned, and monitoring shows latency and error rates flat. The product owner asks for a stronger model. Which observation about the architecture explains the trend and points to the right change?
o: The classification prompt was tuned on the launch data and the model has since begun to overfit to it, so the prompt needs rewriting, with fresh examples drawn from the misrouted claims of the last quarter
The design has no feedback loop; misrouted claims never reach an owner or the evaluation set, so input drift goes uncorrected until users complain

The pinned model version is now outdated relative to the current release and needs to be upgraded to recover accuracy, since newer releases classify insurance language more accurately than the pinned version
The code-based rules have too many branches, and each new claim type increases the probability of a misrouting error
MOCK_STD.e: Flat latency and errors with rising misrouting and no changes is the signature of input drift with no correction mechanism. Models do not "overfit over time" without retraining; the fix is a feedback loop that turns misroutes into eval cases and prompt/rule updates, not a bigger model.

MOCK_STD.q: A pharmaceutical company wants to investigate manufacturing deviations. Each investigation starts from an alert, and the next check depends on what the previous check found: some cases close after two lookups, others require twenty across batch records, equipment logs and supplier certificates. Investigations are audited by regulators, and closing a case incorrectly carries serious consequences. Which pattern and safeguards fit?
o: A fixed workflow that runs all twenty possible checks on every deviation so that the regulator sees a consistent, complete process each time
An agent with read-only tools over the three record systems, a bounded turn and cost budget, full trace logging, and a human quality reviewer who closes each case

An augmented single call with all batch records, equipment logs and supplier certificates attached, producing a closing recommendation in one pass, which keeps the audit trail short and easy for regulators to read
A routing workflow that classifies the alert type and dispatches it to one of five pre-written investigation checklists executed by code
MOCK_STD.e: Input-dependent, unpredictable step counts justify an agent; the regulatory and consequence constraints add read-only tools, budgets, traces and a human closing gate. Running every check always is wasteful and still cannot adapt; a single call cannot perform lookups iteratively.

MOCK_STD.q: A supervisor agent drafts board briefings by delegating to three subagents: one reads financial statements, one summarises risk registers, one checks previous-quarter commitments. End-to-end latency is 11 minutes and the supervisor's context reaches 180,000 tokens before synthesis, because each subagent returns its full source material and the supervisor waits for each in turn. Which change addresses both problems?
o: Replace the three subagents with a single agent that reads all sources sequentially so no synthesis across contexts is needed, accepting a longer runtime in exchange for a simpler architecture

Have each subagent return a structured summary with citations instead of raw material, and run the three independent subagents in parallel, so the supervisor receives four short, comparable inputs before synthesis begins
Give the supervisor a larger context window and enable extended thinking so it can absorb the raw material more reliably
Route the raw material through the Batch API so the supervisor receives it asynchronously and can start synthesis earlier
MOCK_STD.e: Subagent isolation exists to return condensed results and allow parallelism. Raw returns defeat the pattern; a bigger window and Batch API do not fix the design.

MOCK_STD.q: A telecom operator wants a Claude-based assistant for field technicians. Discovery is complete: technicians need step-by-step repair guidance from 900 manuals, must record the parts used, and must not be able to modify work orders. The sponsor's pillar is efficiency (minutes per repair). The team's proposed design ends at "assistant answers the technician". A reviewer asks what is missing. Which two additions complete the end-to-end architecture? (Select TWO)
o: A defined route for low-confidence or out-of-manual questions, escalating to a remote expert with the conversation context attached
A feedback mechanism capturing technician ratings and unresolved cases into the evaluation set and manual-gap backlog
A write tool that allows the assistant to update the work order automatically when a repair is recorded as complete
An evaluator-optimizer loop that critiques each answer three times before showing it to the technician in the field
MOCK_STD.e: Input → processing → output → feedback: the failure route and the loop are the missing stages. Work-order writes violate a stated constraint; a critique loop works against the efficiency pillar.

MOCK_STD.q: A retailer's CFO sponsors a project to cut the cost of answering supplier invoice queries, currently $4.10 per query with a human team. The pilot workflow answers at $0.22 per query with 93% accuracy against a 92% agreed floor and p95 latency of 3 seconds. The engineering team wants to add a second verification pass with a larger model, raising accuracy to 96% and cost to $0.61. Which recommendation aligns with the sponsor's value pillar?
o: Approve the verification pass, because a three-point accuracy gain protects the company from costly supplier disputes, and the CFO can be shown the dispute-cost avoided as a return on the extra spend
Keep the pilot design; it meets the agreed quality floor and the sponsor's pillar is cost, so the extra spend optimises a metric nobody asked for
Approve the verification pass but only on queries above a monetary threshold, and revisit the quality floor with the CFO, so the extra spend is limited to invoices where disputes would be costly
Reject both designs and return to discovery, because a 92% floor is too low for a financial process
MOCK_STD.e: The quality floor is met and the named pillar is cost. Option C is a reasonable engineering idea but changes the agreed criteria without evidence of need; the question asks what aligns with the stated pillar.

MOCK_STD.q: Two business units run their own Claude systems: procurement's agent negotiates supplier terms using its contract database; treasury's agent validates payment schedules against cash-flow forecasts, which procurement is not permitted to see. Leadership wants negotiated terms checked for cash-flow feasibility before signature. Which integration approach respects the data boundary and ownership?
o: Merge both agents into one system with access to both databases so the check happens inside a single reasoning context
Agent-to-agent hand-off: procurement's agent sends the proposed terms to treasury's agent, which returns a feasibility verdict without exposing forecasts

Expose treasury's forecasts through a shared MCP server that procurement's agent can query directly when it needs to check feasibility, with query logging so treasury can audit which forecasts were read
Copy a monthly forecast summary into procurement's system prompt so its agent can evaluate feasibility on its own
